subject: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd

messages.author: 05dd3cef2a986382
messages.subject: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
parts:
Dear laavan community,

I am seeking code examples or guidance for conducting a power analysis with simsem::sim for a simple moderation model involving three continuous latent variables, utilising the MLR estimator and computing the interaction with semTools::indProd.

Despite thorough searches, including reading various vignettes, examples, and online tutorials, I haven't been able to find a suitable guide or example for this specific model type. 

Given the limited guidance from the literature on potential loadings for my specific model, I am aiming to develop a function that examines three conceivable loadings: .8, .7, and .6. These would correspond to error rates of .6, .51, and .64, respectively. My ultimate goal is to estimate these models across a spectrum of sample sizes. 

I would greatly appreciate any assistance or direction on this.
Thank you! 
RS

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
parts:
Rose,
I think that your question is difficult to answer because it is not clear what question you wish to answer with your power study.  If it were me, I would probably be most interested in the power to detect the indirect effect as a defined parameter.  I would probably run separate conditions (separate calls to simsem()) for each of the three loading values.  I would probably generate the data sets within each condition based on a sequence of sample sizes from a minimum to a maximum with a specified length.  This would allow me to plot power against sample size, possibly using a smoothed line such as from the lowess() function.  I do not believe that there are any challenges specific to your model.  As such, you should be safe piecing together code borrowed from various examples in the tutorial.

Keith

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
parts:
Rose,
Sorry, I let my Bayesian prior swamp the data and misread your question as being about mediation instead of moderation.

In the conversation that you cited, Terrence provides a script for simulating the latent interaction and Ed Rigdon provides sample code and a set of slides describing fitting the interaction model.  One strategy might be to follow Terrence's approach just for the indicators of the latent variables, not the interaction, and then use the semTools::inProd() or semTools::orthogonalize() to add the indicators of the interaction to the data set.  Both functions return a data set with the product indicators added to the original variables.  You could then return this augmented data set in your function passed to simsem as the data generation function.

https://groups.google.com/g/lavaan/c/PxFUKcIwPd0/m/-T67JNWL4doJ

If you have doubts about your code, the question is how can you test it.  One strategy would be to use your data generation function outside of simsem, call it on your own and save the data.  Then fit your interaction model to that data and evaluate the parameter recovery.  If you are able to recover the parameters that you used to generate the data, then that suggests that you are on the right track.  Use a large sample size to minimize sampling error for this test.  Choose effects that are clearly distinct from zero.

Terrence's code generates values for the latent variables.  You can leave these in your data without using them in your SE model.  You can plot the interaction using the simulated data to confirm that it looks the way you meant it to.

If your code passes these tests, then I would run a similar model through simsem and look at the mean parameter values across replications, again evaluating these for parameter recovery.  If you can recover the parameters that you put in, that suggests that you have things set up properly.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
parts:
Hi Keith,

I've put together a script for simulating a moderation model using indProd and would appreciate your review (please!)
Model overview: Three latent variables, each with five indicators. Factor loadings: Set at 0.65 for each indicator. Regression coefficients for f3: 0.3 from f1 0.3 from f2 0.1 for the interaction between f1 and f2. I've structured the script to easily adjust factor loadings, coefficients, and to evaluate the power of these regressions. Could you confirm if this approach effectively assesses the power for the specified regression effects?
I will also adjust nrep and N.  

Thank you for your expertise!
Rose


# Function to simulate data with a specific structure of interaction
SEM_sim_with_interaction <- function(N, FL, coefs) {
 
  # Calculate the error variance from the given factor loadings (FL)
  errorVar <- 1 - FL^2
 
  # Define the names for latent factors and manifest variables
  factorNames <- paste0("f", 1:3)
  manifestNames <- paste0("y", 1:15)
 
  # Construct a factor loading matrix (Lambda) with zeros, then fill in given loadings
  Lambda <- matrix(0, nrow = length(manifestNames), ncol = length(factorNames),
                   dimnames = list(manifestNames, factorNames))
  Lambda[1:5, 1] <- FL
  Lambda[6:10, 2] <- FL
  Lambda[11:15, 3] <- FL
 
  # Define the error variance-covariance matrix (Theta) for manifest variables
  Theta <- matrix(0, nrow = length(manifestNames), ncol = length(manifestNames),
                  dimnames = list(manifestNames, manifestNames))
  diag(Theta) <- c(rep(errorVar[1], 5), rep(errorVar[2], 5), rep(errorVar[3], 5))
 
  # Define the mean structure for the latent factors
  Alpha <- rep(0, length(factorNames))
  Tau <- rep(0, length(manifestNames))
  Mu <- Tau + Lambda %*% Alpha
 
  # Define the covariance matrix (Phi) for the first two common latent factors
  Phi <- matrix(1, nrow = 2, ncol = 2, dimnames = list(c("f1", "f2"), c("f1", "f2")))
  Phi[2, 1] <- .4
  Phi[1, 2] <- Phi[2, 1]
 
  # Generate multivariate normal data 
  Kappa <- Alpha[1:nrow(Phi)]
  factors <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = Kappa, Sigma = Phi))
 
  # Calculate the third endogenous latent factor using the coefficients (coefs)
  int3 <- Alpha[3]
  factors$f3 <- int3 + coefs[1]*factors$f1 + coefs[2]*factors$f2 + coefs[3]*factors$f1*factors$f2
  resVar <- 1 - var(factors$f3)
  factors$f3 <- factors$f3 + rnorm(N, sd = sqrt(resVar))
 
  # Generate unique factor data for manifest variables
  uniqueFactors <- data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = Mu, Sigma = Theta))
 
  # Compute the manifest variables by combining common and unique factors
  manifests <- (as.matrix(factors) %*% t(Lambda)) + uniqueFactors
 
  # Create interaction terms for manifest variables using the indProd function
  interaction_data <- indProd(manifests,
                              var1 = c("y1", "y2", "y3", "y4", "y5"),
                              var2 = c("y6", "y7", "y8", "y9", "y10"),
                              doubleMC = TRUE, match = TRUE)
 
  # Return the combined dataset with manifest variables and their interactions
  return(cbind(manifests, interaction_data))
}

# Structural equation model
mod <- '
  # Define latent variables from manifest variables
    f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4 + y5
    f2 =~ y6 + y7 + y8 + y9 + y10
    f3 =~ y11 + y12 + y13 + y14 + y15
 
   # Specify interaction terms for the latent variable
    f_int =~ y1.y6 + y2.y7 + y3.y8 + y4.y9 + y5.y10
 
  # Regression relations among latent variables
    f3 ~ c1*f1 + c2*f2 + c3*f_int
'

# Simulation based on the defined model
Output <- sim(5, model=mod, n=200,
              # 'FL=rep(.65, 5)' specifies that all factor loadings are set to .65 for each of the 5 manifest variables for each latent factor.
              # 'coefs = c(.3,.3,.1)' sets the regression coefficients for the components used to compute f3:
              # - coefs[1] = .3: coefficient for the relationship between f1 and f3 (coefs[1]*factors$f1)
              # - coefs[2] = .3: coefficient for the relationship between f2 and f3 (coefs[2]*factors$f2)
              # - coefs[3] = .1: coefficient for the interaction effect between f1 and f2 on f3 (coefs[3]*factors$f1*factors$f2).
              generate=function(n) SEM_sim_with_interaction(n,
                                                            FL=rep(.65, 5),
                                                            coefs = c(.3,.3,.1)),
              std.lv=TRUE,
              lavaanfun = "sem",
              seed = 4523)

summary(Output)

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: Power analysis, simple moderation, continuous, indProd
parts:
Rose,
I like you coding style, it is easy to read.  I especially liked the use of the anonymous function to pass parameters to the generate parameter to the sim() function.  I tend to use two-space indentation, following Google R coding style, but I found the single indent perfectly readable.

Your code ran for me and I did not catch any red flags.  

5 replications with n=200 is not idea to evaluate parameter recovery.  The mean estimates seem plausible, but one thing that you could do is to run this with a very large sample size fore the sole purpose of evaluating parameter recovery as a means of checking your code.  I don't think that we should ever treat code review as a substitute for code testing.

I had to think about this for a moment but my understanding is that you are fine simulating variables with unit variances and analyzing them with analysis of covariance structure, you would only get into trouble if you standardize the data to force it into a correlation matrix and then analyze it as a covariance matrix, because you would then be treating fixed variances as random.  So, I think that simulating unit variances was a reasonable and safe strategy to simplify the code.  But if you want to maximize the similarity between your power study and the planned analysis, you might consider simulating data based on the observed or anticipated descriptive statistics.

The basic output gives you empirical standard errors.  However, if you are not already aware, simsem offers a number of ancillary functions specific to power studies.  I used the basic getPower() function which showed considerable variability in power cross the parameters of interest (not too surprising with N = 200).

My usual practice is to test the model specification with simulateData() before using it with sim() but I suppose you could accomplish much the same thing with a single replication using the draw() and exportData() functions.  (I have never done that.)  However, if the list of parameters in the sim() ouptut lines up with what you were expecting, your model specification is probably fine.  Here is one convenient way to count them: length(getPower(Output)).

One thing that I like to do, unrelated to the substance of your code, is to provide three-part internal documentation for any function: One line about the purpose of the function, one line about the parameters, and one line about the return value.  The middle line is especially helpful in R code because, to the best of my knowledge, there is no built in way to annotate the parameter types in the function definition syntax itself.  As an example of why this can be helpful, it was not immediately obvious to me whether FL was meant to be scalar or a vector until I read further into the code.

HTH,

Keith
